PRICE INCREASE BREAK-EVEN CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

How many customers can you lose after a price increase?

Paste your items — price, what each unit costs you, units sold — and set the increase. See how much volume you can lose before the raise stops paying, which items can take it, and the customer sensitivity at which it fails.

Nothing is uploaded. The text box is analysed in this browser and never leaves your device. Customer reaction cannot be read from past sales, so you set it and the result shows how much it matters.

1. Paste your items

2. What it found

ItemNew priceCan loseStops paying at elasticityProfit change

Findings

RuleLevelDetail

Prefer a CLI, or want a CI check?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one command — reads a file or stdin:

node cli.mjs analyze items.csv --increase 8
cat items.csv | node cli.mjs analyze - --increase 5 --elasticity 1.5
node cli.mjs analyze items.csv --increase 8 --json --fail-on warn

Get cli.mjs and engine.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install, no network call. More: How much volume can you lose after a price increase?

What's recognised

InputHandling

Costs stay flat, items do not affect each other, and demand follows units × (1 + increase)^-elasticity. Fixed overhead is not modelled.

Common questions

Will this tell me how many customers I will lose?

No. How customers react is the one number nobody can read off past sales. The tool shows how many units you can lose before the raise stops paying, and the elasticity at which that happens, so you can judge whether your customers are that sensitive.

What is elasticity here?

The percentage fall in units sold for each 1% rise in price. 1.0 means a 5% raise loses about 5% of units. Commodity goods with many substitutes are often above 1; specialised services with loyal clients are often below it. 1.0 is a placeholder, not a benchmark.

How do I get the numbers?

Export items from your POS, store or price list: price, what each unit costs you to supply (materials, labour, fees that scale with a sale), and units sold over a recent period. Fixed overhead is left out on purpose, because it does not change when units change.

Does it account for competitors or other items?

No. Each item stands alone and costs stay flat. If a raise on one item pushes customers to another item or a rival, that is outside this arithmetic: test on a few items first.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page runs on the text in your own browser and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads a local file or stdin and makes no network call.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not financial, tax, legal or business advice. It does arithmetic on the rows you paste plus one behavioural assumption you set; it is not a measurement of your customers and not a forecast of what a price change will earn. Test a raise on a few items and compare units sold before rolling it out. Check any contract, price-lock or regulation that limits when you may raise prices.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. The text you paste is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (analyze_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Related tools on the same repo: the Price Elasticity Estimator, the Freelance Rate Increase Calculator, the Clearance Markdown Planner and the Bundle Discount Optimizer.

price-increase-guide.html.text:
Price Increase Break-Even Calculator · guide

How much volume can you lose after a price increase?

Short answer: more than you think when your margin is thin, and less when it is fat. A raise earns extra on every unit you keep and loses the whole unit margin on every unit you lose, so the break-even is set by your margin, not by how nervous the raise feels.

The arithmetic

break-even volume loss = (new price - old price) / (new price - unit cost)

price 100, cost 60, raise 10%  ->  10 / 50  = 20% of units
price 100, cost 90, raise 10%  ->  10 / 20  = 50% of units
price 100, cost 95, raise  2%  ->   2 /  7  = 29% of units

Read it as: the raise is paid for by the units you keep. When the raise is large next to the margin you already earn, each kept unit pays for many lost ones. When the margin is already fat, the same raise barely changes what a unit earns, so losing units hurts quickly. Fixed overhead stays out of it: it does not move when a customer walks away.

Why the answer is a sensitivity, not a number

Past sales show your margin exactly and say nothing about how customers will react. The calculator therefore reports, for every item, the elasticity at which the raise stops paying. If you believe your customers are less sensitive than that, raise; if not, leave it.

Common questions

How much volume can I lose after a price increase?

Divide the dollar raise by the new unit margin: with a unit margin of 40 on a price of 100, a 10% raise lets you lose 10 / 50 = 20% of units before profit falls; at a unit margin of 10 the same raise tolerates 10 / 20 = 50%. Thin-margin items can lose more units.

What elasticity should I assume?

Nobody knows without testing. Treat 1.0 as a neutral placeholder and read the tool's break-even elasticity for each item: if your customers are less sensitive than that number, the raise pays.

Test it

  1. Export items with price, unit cost and units sold.
  2. Paste them into the calculator, or run node cli.mjs analyze items.csv --increase 8.
  3. Raise the items with the largest cushion first, and compare units sold for a few weeks before touching the rest.

No warranty. Provided free and as-is. Not financial, tax, legal or business advice; arithmetic on numbers you supply, not a forecast. Check contracts and rules that limit price changes.
